cur:objects-gandersheim-gospels-cover-as.summary: Within borders of inhabited vine scroll, the ivory shows Christ ascending in a mandorla, lifted by two angels toward the hand of God, while two further angels bow beneath and the Virgin and the apostles gather below, gazing upward. The ivory was later set in a silver-gilt frame. It belongs to the refined Metz school of Carolingian ivory carving.
facts: The Coburg collections describe it as the book cover of the Gandersheim Gospels, Metz ivory of about 860–870, with a silver-gilt frame added in 1555 (inv. Pl.001).

walters:71.297.summary: Carved from a tall curved section of tusk, this ivory shows the Virgin seated with the Christ Child on her lap; he throws his arm round her neck and presses his cheek to hers, while she gazes straight ahead with large, fixed eyes. At the right a standing attendant holds a staff, and a small face appears in the upper corner. The Walters calls it one of the earliest examples of the tender embrace later known in Byzantium as the Eleousa, or Virgin of Tenderness.
facts: The museum suggests the relief was an icon for private devotion, in a monastic or domestic setting, and singles out the large head, fixed gaze and angular drapery as typical of early medieval Christian Egypt.
It is unusually large for an ivory, about 26 cm high, its shape following the curve of the tusk.
It was in Cologne in the 1870s and passed through two Paris sales before Henry Walters bought it in 1905.
walters:71.297.notes: Date 7th–8th century per the Walters (Commons gives 7th century).
